---
title: Define a type
description: Register a type for items no shipped type fits, with the properties Marfa checks on every item of it.
---

This guide registers a type for receipt photos, `app.example.receipt`, built on the image type Marfa ships. [Items and types](/build/items-and-types) explains what a type is and when to build on another.

You need your own Marfa instance, with the CLI signed in to it, as the [Quickstart](/quickstart) leaves you. Make your app a key that may register its own types and write their items:

```bash
marfa keys create --label "Receipts app" --source receipts-app \
  --type-permission "app.example.*=write" --metadata-permission types=write
```

## Write the definition

Keep the definition in a file. Each call on this page sends the file as it stands:

```json title="receipt.json"
{
  "id": "app.example.receipt",
  "parent": "core.file.image",
  "fields": {
    "merchant": { "type": "string", "required": true, "description": "Where the purchase was made" },
    "total": { "type": "number" },
    "currency": { "type": "string", "format": "currency" }
  }
}
```

- **`id`** says who the type is for: `app.<app name>.<type>` for your app's own types, `user.<type>` for types you keep for yourself, or a name of your own, such as `acme.deal`, for types you publish. Name a type with a singular noun, and write words in `snake_case`. [Type rules](/catalog/type-rules#identifier) lists what an identifier must meet.
- **`parent`** makes the type a child of another. A receipt is an image with a merchant and a total, so it takes every property of `core.file.image` as well as its own.
- **`fields`** declares the type's own properties. Each needs a `type`, one of the [field kinds](/catalog/field-kinds). `required` defaults to `false`, an enum needs `enum_values` and an array needs `items_type`. [Field kinds](/catalog/field-kinds#definition) lists every key a field takes.

A property can't share a name with a field every item has, such as `source` or `version` ([reserved field names](/catalog/type-rules#reserved-field-names)). Keep the time the thing happened in the item's own `occurred_at`. [Register a type](/api-reference/types/registerType) lists the rest a type can declare, such as its label, display hints and policies.

Marfa keeps a property the type doesn't declare and serves it back. To refuse one, name the type in the `strict_mode` lever, as [Settings](/run/settings#what-the-enforcement-levers-do) shows.

`marfa types scaffold` prints a definition to start from. It needs no server or key:

```bash
marfa types scaffold app.example.receipt --parent core.file.image \
  --field merchant:string --field total:number --field currency:string \
  --required merchant > receipt.json
```

A field is `NAME:TYPE`, an enum `NAME:enum:one,two`, an array `NAME:array:TYPE` and a [status field](/catalog/field-kinds#status-words) `NAME:status:WORD=GROUP,WORD=GROUP`, such as `stage:status:open=not_started,closed=completed`. The command refuses what registration would refuse, and says why. It can't set a field's `description` or `format`, so add them to the file.

### Make it readable as another type

To make a type readable as another without taking its properties, name that type in `compatible_with`. A recipe whose `title` and `body` are text can be read as a note:

```json title="recipe.json"
{
  "id": "user.recipe",
  "compatible_with": ["core.note"],
  "fields": {
    "title": { "type": "string" },
    "body": { "type": "string" },
    "servings": { "type": "integer" }
  }
}
```

Marfa checks the claim against the [compatibility rules](/catalog/type-rules#compatible-with) when you register or replace the type, and refuses one that doesn't hold with `422 compatible_with_violation`, naming the field. The claim then protects its target: a change to the target that would break it is refused the same way, with the types that claim it in `details.dependent_type_ids`. A compatible type inherits nothing, so a listing of `core.note` leaves recipes out.

A connector's type takes the other route: it names the core type it reads as in `parent`, such as `core.bookmark`, so a listing of the core type includes the connector's items, as [Build a connector](/build/connector) shows.

### Give it a table

When an item holds many small records, such as a receipt's lines, declare a table under `tables` rather than making each record an item. Add this to the definition to give every receipt a `lines` table:

```json title="receipt.json (part)"
"tables": {
  "lines": {
    "order": "position",
    "columns": {
      "position": { "type": "integer", "required": true },
      "description": { "type": "string", "required": true, "searchable": true },
      "amount": { "type": "number", "adds_up": "sum" }
    }
  }
}
```

Each column needs a `type`, and can be `required`, say how it adds up and be `searchable`, so search finds the rows that mention a word. `order` names the column the rows are kept in. [Tables](/build/tables) explains rows, and the contract's [tables](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/tables.md) chapter lists every key a table and a column take.

## Register the type

```bash tab="CLI" tab-group="client"
marfa types register --file receipt.json
```

```http tab="HTTP"
POST /types
Authorization: Bearer $MARFA_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

<the contents of receipt.json>
```

```ts tab="TypeScript"
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const definition = JSON.parse(await readFile("receipt.json", "utf8"));
const { data, error } = await marfa.POST("/types", { body: definition });
```

```swift tab="Swift"
import Foundation
import MarfaAPI

let api = Client(server)
let definition = try JSONDecoder().decode(
    Components.Schemas.TypeDefinitionInput.self, from: Data(contentsOf: receiptURL))
let registered = try await api.register(itemType: definition)
```

In the TypeScript examples, `marfa` is a client made as [the TypeScript SDK](/typescript-sdk#create-a-client) shows. In the Swift examples, `api` is a `Client` made as [the Swift SDK](/swift-sdk/server-calls#the-api-client) shows, and `receiptURL` is the file's location. Marfa answers `201` with the type as it stored it:

```json title="Response" status="201"
{
  "id": "app.example.receipt",
  "version": 0,
  "fields": {
    "merchant": { "type": "string", "description": "Where the purchase was made", "required": true },
    "total": { "type": "number" },
    "currency": { "type": "string", "format": "currency" }
  },
  "parent": "core.file.image",
  "label": "Receipt",
  "plural": "Receipts",
  "provenance": {
    "origin": "user",
    "created_by": { "kind": "key", "id": "01a1f12f-c7d0-7a21-9f6b-4d2c8e1a3b57", "name": "Receipts app" }
  }
}
```

Marfa made the `label` and `plural` from the identifier, and `provenance.created_by` names who registered the type. A replacement keeps that creator. The `version` is **yours to keep**: Marfa stores the number you send, 0 when you send none, and never changes it. An identifier that is already registered is refused `409 type_exists`.

`marfa types get app.example.receipt` ([Get a type](/api-reference/types/getType)) answers the type with the properties it inherits, such as `blob_ref`, `mime_type`, `width` and `height`. An item must hold **every required property along the chain**, so a receipt needs a `blob_ref`, a `mime_type` and a `merchant`. A write that lacks one is refused `400 invalid_properties`, naming it.

A type can also set [`display_hints`](/catalog/display-hints): the field that names an item, the field that holds its Markdown text, and an `icon`, an Iconify ID such as `lucide:receipt`. Each one comes from the nearest type that sets it, so a receipt that sets only an icon keeps the title its parent names. The server and a device [name an item](/catalog/display-hints#names-and-previews) from these hints by one rule.

Once the type is registered, [change or delete it](/build/change-a-type) as your app grows.

## What your key needs

Each operation needs a key whose type map grants write on the type's identifier, plus a grant of its own:

| Operation | Also needs |
| --- | --- |
| Register | `metadata.types:write`, the `types` entry of the key's metadata map (`--metadata-permission types=write`). |
| Replace | `metadata.types:write` when the change only adds optional properties no item holds a value under, or changes the label, the `plural`, a description, the display hints, the version or a field's `label`. Any other change, such as removing a property or making one required, needs the `schema.write` permission. |
| Delete | `schema.write`. |

A new parent or `compatible_with` target that isn't a type Marfa ships also needs write on that type. One the type already names doesn't, so a connector can update its type after its permissions narrow. A missing write is refused `403 type_not_permitted`, and `details.grant` names it.

A replacement that needs `schema.write`, from a key without it, is refused `403 forbidden`, and `details.changes` lists each part that needs it, such as `fields.total`. Send those parts with a key that holds `schema.write`. [Manage keys](/run/manage-keys) shows how to give a key its maps and permissions.

The rules behind this guide are in the [types](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/types.md) chapter of the contract.
